Visualizing Customer Segmentation with K-Means Clustering

A Marketing Analytics Approach to Grouping Similar Customers

Chengxu Liu

MGTA 495

2026-05-29

Not All Customers Are the Same

Marketing problem:

A brand should not send the same message to every customer.

Some customers buy often. Some spend more. Some need a discount to come back.

What Clustering Does

Clustering groups customers who look similar.

In this example, we use two features:

  • purchase frequency
  • average spending

The goal is to find natural customer segments.

How K-Means Moves

Step 1

Start with rough centers.

Step 2

Assign customers to the closest center.

Final

Repeat until the groups are stable.

Practical Problem 1: Too Many Variables

Problem: K-means depends on distance.

With too many variables, distance becomes harder to trust.

This is called the curse of dimensionality.

Data size What happens
2 variables Distance is easy to see
10+ variables Many points may look similarly far apart
Result Clusters can become less meaningful

Practical fixes:

  • Select only useful variables
  • Standardize before clustering
  • Use PCA to reduce dimensions

Practical Problem 2: Binary Variables

Can we use 0/1 variables?

Sometimes yes, but we need to be careful.

Examples:

  • email subscriber
  • used coupon
  • app user
Case What to watch for
Balanced 0/1 Usually more usable
Very rare 1s May add little value
Many binary variables K-means may not fit well

Better option: For mixed data, consider k-prototypes or a mixed-data distance measure.

Why This Helps Marketers

Segment What it means Possible action
High spending Valuable customers Loyalty reward
Frequent buyers Already engaged Cross-sell message
Low engagement Need a push Discount or reminder

Main idea: Customer segmentation helps marketers send better messages to the right people.

K-means is not magic. It is just a visual way to find similar customers.
